cards.front: What is the agentic loop lifecycle in Claude-based systems?
cards.back: Send request → inspect stop_reason → if tool_use, execute tools and append results to history → repeat until stop_reason is end_turn.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/agents-and-tools/agent-sdk/overview

cards.front: 12% of support cases skip get_customer and call lookup_order by name only, causing wrong refunds. Most effective fix?
cards.back: Programmatic prerequisite: block lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns a verified customer ID.
cards.rationale: Financial identity steps need deterministic enforcement; prompts and few-shot alone are probabilistic.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4; Sample Q1

cards.front: Single agent with many tools vs coordinator + specialized subagents for a research pipeline?
cards.back: Coordinator + subagents when work decomposes (search, analyze, synthesize), needs isolated context, and clear failure boundaries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Why must a coordinator not invent subagent outputs without tool results?
cards.back: Breaks provenance and reliability; delegate via Task tool and pass explicit context—never hallucinate worker findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3

cards.front: When should an agentic loop continue versus terminate?
cards.back: Continue when stop_reason is tool_use; terminate when stop_reason is end_turn.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: Name three anti-patterns for deciding when an agentic loop should terminate.
cards.back: Parsing natural language for completion; arbitrary iteration caps as primary stop; treating assistant text as completion signal.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: When should you use model-driven tool selection versus pre-configured decision trees?
cards.back: Model-driven: Claude picks tools from context each turn. Decision trees/forced sequences bypass model reasoning—use only when deterministic ordering is required.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: Why should you append tool results to conversation history between loop iterations?
cards.back: So the model can reason about new information and choose the next action based on actual tool output.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: What is hub-and-spoke multi-agent architecture?
cards.back: Coordinator manages all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information routing; subagents do not talk directly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Do subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history?
cards.back: No—subagents operate with isolated context; parent history is not inherited automatically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3

cards.front: A report on 'AI in creative industries' covers only visual arts. Logs show the coordinator assigned digital art, graphic design, and photography only. What is the root cause?
cards.back: Coordinator task decomposition too narrow—subagents executed correctly but were assigned incomplete scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2; Sample Q7
cards.rationale: Coordinator logs show decomposition into only visual-arts subtasks—subagents succeeded within narrow assignments. Downstream agents are not the root cause; synthesis, search, and analysis worked within assigned scope.

cards.front: How should a coordinator select which subagents to invoke?
cards.back: Analyze query requirements and dynamically select needed subagents—not always route through the full pipeline.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2
cards.rationale: The coordinator should analyze the query and invoke only needed subagents. Always running the full pipeline wastes latency and context.

cards.front: How should you partition research scope across subagents to reduce duplication?
cards.back: Assign distinct subtopics or source types per agent (e.g., web vs documents vs synthesis)—not overlapping queries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2
cards.rationale: Assign distinct subtopics or source types (for example web vs documents vs synthesis) so subagents do not duplicate overlapping queries.

cards.front: What is an iterative refinement loop in multi-agent research?
cards.back: Coordinator evaluates synthesis for gaps, re-delegates to search/analysis with targeted queries, re-invokes synthesis until coverage is sufficient.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Why route all subagent communication through the coordinator?
cards.back: Observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2
cards.rationale: Hub-and-spoke routing through the coordinator gives observability, consistent error handling, and controlled information flow; subagents should not talk directly.

cards.front: What tool spawns subagents in the Agent SDK, and what must allowedTools include?
cards.back: The Task tool; allowedTools must include "Task" for a coordinator to invoke subagents.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: How should you pass prior agent findings to a synthesis subagent?
cards.back: Include complete findings directly in the subagent prompt (search results, document analysis)—not rely on automatic inheritance.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3
cards.rationale: Subagents do not inherit parent history. Put complete prior findings in the prompt or they will invent or omit evidence.

cards.front: When passing context between agents, what practice preserves attribution?
cards.back: Use structured formats separating content from metadata (URLs, document names, page numbers).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3
cards.rationale: Separate claims from metadata (URLs, document names, page numbers) so attribution survives synthesis instead of collapsing into an uncited summary.

cards.front: How should you spawn parallel subagents to lower latency?
cards.back: Emit multiple Task tool calls in a single coordinator response—not separate turns per subagent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3
cards.rationale: Multiple Task calls in one coordinator response run in parallel. Sequential turns add a full round-trip of latency per subagent.

cards.front: Should coordinator prompts specify step-by-step procedures or research goals?
cards.back: Specify research goals and quality criteria—enables subagent adaptability vs rigid procedural scripts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3
cards.rationale: Goal-and-quality-criteria prompts let subagents adapt. Step-by-step scripts break when the evidence does not match the assumed procedure.

cards.front: What does AgentDefinition configure for each subagent type?
cards.back: Description, system prompt, and tool restrictions per subagent role.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: What is fork-based session management in multi-agent workflows?
cards.back: Create independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches (e.g., two testing strategies).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3, 1.7

cards.front: When should you use programmatic enforcement (hooks, gates) instead of prompt-based workflow ordering?
cards.back: Prompts have non-zero failure rate; programmatic gates give deterministic compliance when identity verification or financial ops require it.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: Customer message has multiple concerns (billing + return). How should the agent investigate?
cards.back: Decompose into distinct items, investigate each in parallel using shared context, then synthesize a unified resolution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4
cards.rationale: Task 1.4: split multi-concern messages, investigate items in parallel with shared context, then synthesize one resolution—do not treat mixed issues as a single thread.

cards.front: What must a structured human handoff include when escalating mid-process?
cards.back: Customer details, root cause analysis, recommended actions—humans may lack full conversation transcript.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: What fields should a structured handoff include for a refund escalation?
cards.back: Customer ID, root cause, refund amount, recommended action.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4
cards.rationale: Humans often lack the transcript. Hand off customer ID, root cause, refund amount, and a recommended action so they can act immediately.

cards.front: What does a PostToolUse hook do?
cards.back: Intercepts tool results after execution to transform/normalize data before the model processes them.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: MCP tools return mixed timestamp formats (Unix, ISO 8601). Best approach before agent reasoning?
cards.back: PostToolUse hook to normalize heterogeneous formats into a consistent representation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5
cards.rationale: PostToolUse normalizes timestamps and status codes before the model reasons. Prompting the model to 'handle mixed formats' is probabilistic.

cards.front: A business rule blocks refunds over $500 and requires escalation. Should you use hooks or prompt instructions?
cards.back: Tool call interception hook—hooks guarantee compliance; prompts are probabilistic.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5
cards.rationale: hooks guarantee compliance; prompts are probabilistic.

cards.front: What is the purpose of tool-call interception hooks?
cards.back: Block policy-violating outgoing tool calls (e.g., large refunds) and redirect to alternative workflows (human escalation).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5

cards.front: When should you use a fixed sequential pipeline versus dynamic adaptive decomposition?
cards.back: Sequential pipelines for predictable multi-step reviews; dynamic decomposition for open-ended investigation that adapts to intermediate findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: A 14-file PR review misses bugs and gives contradictory feedback. How should you restructure the review?
cards.back: Per-file local analysis passes, then a separate cross-file integration pass—avoids attention dilution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6; Sample Q12
cards.rationale: Split reviews into per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass—fixes attention dilution across many files. Splitting PRs burdens developers; larger context does not fix attention quality; consensus across passes would suppress intermittently caught bugs.

cards.front: You need to add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase. What decomposition strategy should you use?
cards.back: Map structure → identify high-impact areas → prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 1.6: Map structure → identify high-impact areas → prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered.

cards.front: What is prompt chaining for task decomposition?
cards.back: Break work into sequential focused steps (e.g., analyze each file, then cross-file integration pass).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: How do you resume a named session in Claude Code?
cards.back: Use --resume with a session name to continue a specific prior conversation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: What is fork_session used for?
cards.back: Create parallel exploration branches from a shared baseline (e.g., compare two refactoring or testing strategies).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7

cards.front: After the code has changed, when should you resume a session versus start fresh?
cards.back: Resume when prior context is mostly valid; start fresh with injected summary when prior tool results are stale—more reliable than stale resumes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7
cards.rationale: Resume when prior context is still valid. If tool results are stale after code changes, start fresh with an injected summary rather than a stale session.

cards.front: When resuming a session after specific files changed, what should you tell the agent?
cards.back: Inform about specific file changes for targeted re-analysis—not require full re-exploration of the codebase.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.7
cards.rationale: Tell the resumed session which files changed so it re-analyzes those paths instead of re-exploring the whole codebase.

cards.front: Synthesis needs simple fact-checks 85% of the time and complex search 15% of the time. How do you reduce latency without over-provisioning?
cards.back: Give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups; complex verifications still delegate through coordinator to search agent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2–1.3; Sample Q9
cards.rationale: Scoped verify_fact on synthesis covers the common simple fact-check case while complex work stays with search via coordinator—least privilege. End-of-pass batching creates blocking dependencies; giving synthesis all search tools over-provisions; speculative caching cannot predict verification needs.

cards.front: Which primary domains do the Customer Support and Multi-Agent Research scenarios share?
cards.back: Both list D1 (Agentic Architecture), D2 (Tool Design & MCP), and D5 (Context Management & Reliability).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What are the four coordinator responsibilities in hub-and-spoke orchestration?
cards.back: Task decomposition, delegation to subagents, result aggregation, and dynamic selection of which subagents to invoke.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: Do subagents share memory across separate Task invocations?
cards.back: No—each invocation is isolated; context must be explicitly provided in the prompt every time.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.3

cards.front: What is attention dilution in multi-step agent workflows?
cards.back: Processing too many items in one pass (many files, broad topics) reduces depth and consistency—some areas get superficial treatment while others are detailed.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: What is an adaptive investigation plan for task decomposition?
cards.back: Generate subtasks based on what is discovered at each step—not a fixed pipeline decided upfront.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.6

cards.front: In a PostToolUse hook, which heterogeneous MCP fields should you normalize before the model sees them?
cards.back: Timestamps (Unix vs ISO 8601), numeric status codes, and other inconsistent formats from different backend tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.5
cards.rationale: Task 1.5: normalize Unix vs ISO timestamps, numeric status codes, and other inconsistent MCP fields in PostToolUse before they enter model context.

cards.front: The web search subagent times out. What error context should you send to the coordinator?
cards.back: Structured error context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.2; Sample Q8
cards.rationale: Structured error context enables coordinator recovery (retry, alternate query, partial results). Generic retry status hides context; marking failure as success blocks recovery; terminating the whole workflow is unnecessary when partial progress exists.

cards.front: Agent skips identity verification before refunds. Why is a routing classifier the wrong first fix?
cards.back: Problem is tool ordering, not tool availability—a classifier limits which tools exist but does not enforce get_customer before lookup_order/refund.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4; Sample Q1

cards.front: When should a support agent escalate to a human instead of continuing the agentic loop?
cards.back: Customer explicitly requests a human, policy is silent or requires an exception, or the agent cannot make meaningful progress—not self-reported confidence scores.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Customer Support scenario
cards.rationale: Exam Guide task 5.2 names those three triggers. Sample Q3 rejects confidence thresholds and sentiment as proxies for complexity; identity ambiguity is resolved by asking for more identifiers, not by treating a confidence score as a stop signal.

cards.front: For the Developer Productivity scenario, which domains are primary, and what is the D1 focus?
cards.back: D2 (tools/MCP), D3 (Claude Code), D1 (delegation/orchestration with built-in tools + MCP servers).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What typical subagent roles appear in a multi-agent research pipeline (Exam Scenario 3)?
cards.back: Web search, document analysis, synthesis of findings, and report generation—coordinator delegates each role.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 3; D1, Task 1.2

cards.front: A subagent catches a timeout and returns empty results marked successful. Why is that wrong?
cards.back: Suppresses failure—coordinator cannot recover, retry, or annotate coverage gaps; risks incomplete research output.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: A subagent timeout terminates the entire research workflow. Why is that wrong?
cards.back: Single failures often recoverable with partial results, alternate queries, or gap annotation—unnecessary full termination.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: When is prompt-based workflow guidance enough, and when do you need programmatic gates or hooks?
cards.back: Prompts suffice for soft ordering and preferences; programmatic enforcement when business rules need deterministic compliance (identity before money, refund caps).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4–1.5

cards.front: A subagent retries a timeout internally, then returns generic 'search unavailable' to the coordinator. What information is missing?
cards.back: Hides failure type, attempted query, and partial results—coordinator cannot make informed recovery decisions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q8

cards.front: Which two stop_reason values drive agentic loop control?
cards.back: tool_use (continue loop—execute tools and append results) and end_turn (terminate and present response).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1; Appendix

cards.front: Why should you not give the synthesis agent all web search tools just to eliminate coordinator round-trips?
cards.back: Over-provisions synthesis—violates separation of concerns and role-specific tool scoping; use scoped tools for common cases only.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1; Sample Q9
cards.rationale: Scoped verify_fact on synthesis covers the common simple fact-check case while complex work stays with search via coordinator—least privilege. End-of-pass batching creates blocking dependencies; giving synthesis all search tools over-provisions; speculative caching cannot predict verification needs.

cards.front: What is a programmatic prerequisite gate in a multi-step agent workflow?
cards.back: Code or hook that blocks downstream tool calls until a prerequisite step completes (e.g., no refund until verified customer ID).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: What does MCP (Model Context Protocol) provide to Claude agents?
cards.back: A standard way for AI clients to discover and invoke tools, resources, and prompts from external servers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2
https://modelcontextprotocol.io/introduction

cards.front: What is the primary mechanism LLMs use to select among similar tools?
cards.back: Tool descriptions—minimal descriptions lead to unreliable selection when tools overlap.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Agent calls get_customer for order queries (#12345) instead of lookup_order. Both have minimal descriptions. Best first fix?
cards.back: Expand each tool description: input formats, example queries, edge cases, and when to use vs similar tools.
cards.rationale: Descriptions are the primary selection mechanism; few-shot and routing layers don't fix inadequate descriptions first.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: What should effective tool descriptions include beyond a one-line summary?
cards.back: Expected inputs, outputs, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use vs similar alternatives.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: analyze_content and analyze_document have near-identical descriptions. Likely result?
cards.back: Tool misrouting—the model cannot reliably distinguish overlapping tools with ambiguous descriptions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Generic analyze_content overlaps with analyze_document. How should you rename or fix the tools?
cards.back: Rename to purpose-specific names (e.g., extract_web_results) with web-specific descriptions that eliminate overlap.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1
cards.rationale: Rename overlapping tools to purpose-specific names (for example extract_web_results) and write web-specific descriptions so selection is unambiguous.

cards.front: One generic analyze_document tool does too much. How should you split it?
cards.back: Purpose-specific tools with clear contracts: extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 2.1: Purpose-specific tools with clear contracts: extract_data_points, summarize_content, verify_claim_against_source.

cards.front: How can system prompt wording undermine well-written tool descriptions?
cards.back: Keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations that override description clarity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Tool selection is still wrong after improving descriptions. What should you check next?
cards.back: Review system prompt for keyword-sensitive instructions that might override tool descriptions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1
cards.rationale: After descriptions are fixed, check the system prompt. Keyword-sensitive instructions can create unintended tool associations that override good descriptions.

cards.front: Why is exposing one mega-tool that 'does anything on GitHub' a problem?
cards.back: Harder correct selection, weak error semantics, and excessive blast radius if mis-invoked.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: Similar tools misroute. Why is consolidating into lookup_entity not the best first step?
cards.back: Valid architecture but higher effort; immediate problem is inadequate descriptions—expand those first (Sample Q2).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: How should MCP tools communicate failures back to the agent?
cards.back: The isError flag on tool results, plus structured error metadata—not raw stack traces or generic messages.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Which four MCP error categories does the exam distinguish?
cards.back: Transient (timeouts, unavailability), validation (invalid input), business (policy violations), permission (access denied).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Why is returning generic 'Operation failed' for all tool errors a problem?
cards.back: Prevents the agent from choosing appropriate recovery—retry, explain to user, escalate, or accept empty results.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: Name three structured error metadata fields for MCP tools.
cards.back: errorCategory (transient/validation/permission/business), isRetryable boolean, and human-readable description.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2
cards.rationale: Task 2.2 wants structured metadata: errorCategory, isRetryable, and a human-readable description so the agent can retry, explain, or stop.

cards.front: How should you design the error response for a business-rule violation (for example, a refund over the policy limit)?
cards.back: isRetryable: false, customer-friendly explanation so the agent can communicate appropriately—not retry endlessly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 2.2: isRetryable: false, customer-friendly explanation so the agent can communicate appropriately—not retry endlessly.

cards.front: Access failure (timeout) vs valid empty result (no matches)—how should tools report differently?
cards.back: Access failure: structured error with retry guidance. Valid empty: successful response indicating no matches—not an error.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: When a subagent hits a transient failure, when should it retry locally versus propagate to the coordinator?
cards.back: Retry locally when possible; propagate only unresolved errors with partial results and what was attempted.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 2.2: Retry locally when possible; propagate only unresolved errors with partial results and what was attempted.

cards.front: A tool returns an ambiguous error from an external API. How should the tool layer behave?
cards.back: Structured error payload (category, message, retryable flag)—not raw stack traces or silent failure.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2
cards.rationale: Translate ambiguous API failures into category, message, and retryable flag. Raw stack traces and silent failures both block recovery.

cards.front: Why does giving an agent 18 tools instead of 4–5 hurt reliability?
cards.back: Increases decision complexity and degrades tool selection accuracy.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: The synthesis agent attempts web searches. What tool-design issue is likely?
cards.back: Agent has tools outside its specialization—scoped access should limit synthesis to synthesis-appropriate tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: What is scoped tool access for subagents?
cards.back: Each agent gets only tools for its role, plus limited cross-role tools for specific high-frequency needs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3

cards.front: What are the three tool_choice configuration options on the Claude API?
cards.back: "auto" (model may return text), "any" (must call a tool), and forced selection {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; Appendix

cards.front: When should you set tool_choice to "any"?
cards.back: When you need guaranteed tool invocation instead of conversational text—e.g., unknown document type among multiple extraction schemas.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3
cards.rationale: tool_choice "any" forces a tool call (the model may choose which). Use it when you need structured extraction and the document type is unknown.

cards.front: You must run extract_metadata before enrichment tools. How should you set tool_choice?
cards.back: Force specific tool first with {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, then process enrichment in follow-up turns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 2.3: Force specific tool first with {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"}, then process enrichment in follow-up turns.

cards.front: Replace generic fetch_url with what kind of constrained tool?
cards.back: Purpose-specific tool like load_document that validates document URLs and rejects non-document URLs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 2.3: Purpose-specific tool like load_document that validates document URLs and rejects non-document URLs.

cards.front: Synthesis often needs simple fact-checks. What scoped cross-role tool pattern should you use?
cards.back: Provide verify_fact for high-frequency simple lookups; route complex verification through coordinator to search agent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; D1 Sample Q9
cards.rationale: Scoped verify_fact on synthesis covers the common simple fact-check case while complex work stays with search via coordinator—least privilege. End-of-pass batching creates blocking dependencies; giving synthesis all search tools over-provisions; speculative caching cannot predict verification needs.

cards.front: A refund tool should run only after verified identity. What tool-design choice enforces that?
cards.back: Least privilege: narrow tool exposure or refund tool requiring verified session token from prior identity tool.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; Customer Support scenario
cards.rationale: Least privilege: do not expose refund until identity is verified, or require a verified session token from get_customer. Prompts cannot guarantee ordering.

cards.front: How do project-level and user-level MCP server configurations differ?
cards.back: Project .mcp.json for shared team tooling (version controlled); user ~/.claude.json for personal/experimental servers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: How do you store a GitHub token for a team MCP server without committing secrets?
cards.back: Environment variable expansion in .mcp.json (e.g., ${GITHUB_TOKEN}) with secrets in env—not in the repo.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4
cards.rationale: Put ${GITHUB_TOKEN} (or similar) in project .mcp.json and keep the secret in the environment so the repo never contains credentials.

cards.front: When are MCP tools from multiple servers available to the agent?
cards.back: All configured servers are discovered at connection time—tools from all servers are available simultaneously.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: When should you use MCP resources instead of MCP tools?
cards.back: Resources expose content catalogs (issue summaries, doc hierarchies, DB schemas) to reduce exploratory tool calls.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4

cards.front: The agent prefers Grep over a more capable MCP search tool. How do you fix that?
cards.back: Enhance MCP tool descriptions to explain capabilities and outputs in detail so the model understands when MCP beats built-ins.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4
cards.rationale: If Grep wins over a richer MCP search tool, the MCP description is too weak. Spell out capabilities and outputs so the model knows when MCP is better.

cards.front: You need Jira integration. Should you use a community MCP server or a custom one?
cards.back: Prefer existing community MCP for standard integrations (Jira); custom servers for team-specific workflows.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4
cards.rationale: Use a community MCP for standard SaaS (Jira). Reserve custom servers for team-specific workflows the community server cannot cover.

cards.front: When should you prefer custom MCP over built-in Claude Code tools?
cards.back: MCP for external systems (GitHub, DB, SaaS) or sharing tools across clients; built-ins for local repo operations.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4–2.5

cards.front: What is the primary use case for built-in Grep versus Glob?
cards.back: Grep: search file contents for patterns (function names, errors, imports). Glob: match file paths by name/extension patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Which built-in tool finds all test files named *.test.tsx anywhere in the repo?
cards.back: Glob with pattern like **/*.test.tsx.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5
cards.rationale: Glob matches file paths. **/*.test.tsx finds tests by name anywhere; Grep searches file contents, not filenames.

cards.front: Which built-in tool finds all callers of a function across the codebase?
cards.back: Grep to search file contents for the function name/reference patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5
cards.rationale: Callers are content matches. Grep for the function name; Glob would only find files whose names happen to match.

cards.front: When should you use Edit versus Read plus Write?
cards.back: Edit for targeted changes with unique anchor text; Read + Write when Edit fails due to non-unique matches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: What is the best incremental pattern for exploring a codebase?
cards.back: Grep for entry points → Read to follow imports and trace flows—not read all files upfront.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5
cards.rationale: Start with Grep for entry points, then Read along imports. Loading every file upfront wastes context and dilutes attention.

cards.front: How do you trace usage across wrapper modules that export many names?
cards.back: Identify all exported names first, then Grep for each name across the codebase.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5
cards.rationale: Wrapper modules re-export many names. List exports first, then Grep each name so you do not miss aliased callers.

cards.front: Which three exam scenarios list D2 as a primary domain?
cards.back: Customer Support, Multi-Agent Research, and Developer Productivity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What MCP tools appear in the Customer Support scenario (Exam Scenario 1)?
cards.back: get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human—backend integration via custom MCP tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1

cards.front: What built-in tools appear in the Developer Productivity scenario (Exam Scenario 4)?
cards.back: Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob—plus MCP server integrations for external systems.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 4

cards.front: Why is adding a keyword-routing layer that parses user input each turn often the wrong way to improve tool selection?
cards.back: Over-engineered—bypasses LLM NLU; fix descriptions first; routing doesn't solve ordering or description gaps.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: How do MCP tools and MCP resources divide responsibility?
cards.back: Tools perform actions (fetch, update, search); resources expose catalogs and static context (schemas, doc trees) to cut exploratory calls.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.4; Appendix in-scope

cards.front: Why should error results include structured isRetryable metadata?
cards.back: Lets the agent retry transient failures and avoid wasted retries on non-retryable business or validation errors.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2

cards.front: When should you use the built-in Bash tool versus Grep?
cards.back: Bash for shell commands and scripted operations; Grep for searching file contents for patterns across the codebase.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5; Scenario 4; Appendix

cards.front: What can the model return when tool_choice is "auto"?
cards.back: The model may respond with conversational text instead of calling a tool—no guaranteed tool invocation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.3; D4 Task 4.3

cards.front: Similar tools misroute. Why is adding 5–8 few-shot tool-selection examples the wrong first step?
cards.back: Adds token overhead without fixing root cause—inadequate tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1; Sample Q2

cards.front: How does the built-in Edit tool modify files?
cards.back: Targeted modifications using unique text matching as anchor—fails when anchor text is not unique.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.5

cards.front: Which errorCategory should you use when a policy violation blocks a refund?
cards.back: Business error with isRetryable: false and customer-friendly explanation—not transient or permission.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.2
cards.rationale: Policy violations are business errors: isRetryable false plus a customer-friendly explanation. They are not transient timeouts or permission denials.

cards.front: What is CLAUDE.md in Claude Code workflows?
cards.back: Project instructions and context Claude Code loads to align behavior, conventions, and constraints.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview

cards.front: What are the three levels of the CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy?
cards.back: User (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md), project (.claude/CLAUDE.md or root CLAUDE.md), and directory-level (subdirectory CLAUDE.md files).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: A new teammate does not receive team coding standards in Claude Code. What is the likely cause?
cards.back: Instructions are in user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md—not shared via version control; move to project-level config.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1
cards.rationale: User-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md is not in git. Team standards belong in project CLAUDE.md so clones pick them up.

cards.front: What is @import syntax in CLAUDE.md?
cards.back: References external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular—import standards files relevant to each package.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: A monolithic CLAUDE.md is hard to maintain. How should you reorganize it?
cards.back: Split into focused files in .claude/rules/ (e.g., testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1
cards.rationale: Split a monolithic CLAUDE.md into focused files under .claude/rules/ (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md) instead of one huge always-loaded file.

cards.front: Claude Code behaves inconsistently across sessions. How do you diagnose which config is loaded?
cards.back: Use /memory to verify which memory files are loaded and what context is active.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1
cards.rationale: /memory shows which memory files are loaded. Use it when behavior drifts across sessions because the wrong CLAUDE.md layer is active.

cards.front: Why is it a problem to skip a shared project CLAUDE.md when multiple developers use Claude Code?
cards.back: Inconsistent conventions, duplicated prompt context, and drift in how the agent edits code across teammates.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.1

cards.front: Where should you create a team /review slash command so every developer gets it on clone?
cards.back: .claude/commands/ in the project repository—version-controlled and shared on clone/pull.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2; Sample Q4
cards.rationale: Project slash commands live in .claude/commands/ and are version-controlled for the team. ~/.claude/commands/ is personal; CLAUDE.md holds instructions not command definitions; .claude/config.json is not the Claude Code command mechanism.

cards.front: How do project-scoped and user-scoped slash commands differ?
cards.back: .claude/commands/ in repo (shared via git) vs ~/.claude/commands/ (personal, not version controlled).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: Name three Skill frontmatter options in .claude/skills/SKILL.md.
cards.back: context: fork, allowed-tools, and argument-hint.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: A skill produces verbose codebase analysis. Which frontmatter option isolates that output?
cards.back: context: fork—runs skill in isolated sub-agent context so output doesn't pollute main conversation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2
cards.rationale: runs skill in isolated sub-agent context so output doesn't pollute main conversation.

cards.front: A skill should only write files, not run destructive shell commands. Which frontmatter option enforces that?
cards.back: allowed-tools restricting tool access during skill execution (e.g., file write operations only).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2
cards.rationale: allowed-tools in skill frontmatter limits what the skill can invoke—for example file writes only, so it cannot run destructive shell commands.

cards.front: A developer invokes a skill without required arguments. Which frontmatter option helps?
cards.back: argument-hint prompts for required parameters when the skill is invoked without them.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 3.2: argument-hint prompts for required parameters when the skill is invoked without them.

cards.front: When should you use Skills versus CLAUDE.md?
cards.back: Skills: on-demand task-specific workflows. CLAUDE.md: always-loaded universal standards for the project.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2

cards.front: How do you customize a skill for yourself without affecting teammates?
cards.back: Create personal variants in ~/.claude/skills/ with different names—not in shared project skills.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2
cards.rationale: not in shared project skills.

cards.front: How do .claude/rules/ path-specific rules activate?
cards.back: YAML frontmatter paths field with glob patterns—rules load only when editing matching files.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Test files sit as Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx. How do you apply test conventions automatically?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ with glob paths like **/*.test.tsx—applies by file type across all directories.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6
cards.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob patterns apply conventions by file path—including tests spread across directories. Root CLAUDE.md relies on inference; skills need invocation; per-directory CLAUDE.md cannot cover scattered test files.

cards.front: React, API, and DB areas need different conventions; tests scattered everywhere. Best maintainable approach?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter glob patterns (e.g., paths: ["**/*.test.tsx"], ["src/api/**/*"])—not inference from one monolithic CLAUDE.md.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6
cards.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob patterns apply conventions by file path—including tests spread across directories. Root CLAUDE.md relies on inference; skills need invocation; per-directory CLAUDE.md cannot cover scattered test files.

cards.front: For scattered test files, when should you use path-specific rules versus subdirectory CLAUDE.md?
cards.back: Path-specific glob rules apply by file pattern anywhere in the tree; subdirectory CLAUDE.md is directory-bound.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: What is the benefit of path-scoped rules loading only for matching files?
cards.back: Reduces irrelevant context and token usage—conventions apply only when relevant.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: You need to restructure a monolith into microservices across dozens of files. Which approach should you take first?
cards.back: Plan mode: explore codebase, understand dependencies, design approach before making changes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4; Sample Q5
cards.rationale: Plan mode fits large architectural work with exploration before edits. Direct execution risks rework when dependencies are unknown; upfront rigid instructions skip necessary discovery; switching only if complexity emerges ignores stated large-scale scope.

cards.front: When should you use plan mode versus direct execution?
cards.back: Plan mode: large-scale, multi-file, architectural, multiple valid approaches. Direct execution: simple, well-scoped single changes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: For a single-file bug fix with a clear stack trace, should you use plan mode or direct execution?
cards.back: Direct execution—well-understood change with clear scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4
cards.rationale: well-understood change with clear scope.

cards.front: What is the Explore subagent used for in Claude Code?
cards.back: Isolates verbose discovery output and returns summaries—preserves main conversation context during exploration.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4

cards.front: A library migration affects 45+ files. What workflow pattern should you use?
cards.back: Plan mode for investigation and design, then direct execution to implement the planned approach.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4
cards.rationale: Plan mode for investigation and design on a 45+ file migration, then direct execution to implement the agreed plan.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to start a monolith-to-microservices split in direct execution and switch to plan only if complexity emerges?
cards.back: Complexity is already stated—plan first prevents costly rework from late-discovered dependencies.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4; Sample Q5

cards.front: A natural-language transformation spec produces inconsistent code. What is the best fix?
cards.back: Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples showing expected transformations.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 3.5: Provide 2–3 concrete input/output examples showing expected transformations.

cards.front: What is the test-driven iteration pattern with Claude Code?
cards.back: Write tests first (behavior, edge cases, performance), then iterate by sharing test failures to guide fixes.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: What is the interview pattern in Claude Code workflows?
cards.back: Have Claude ask clarifying questions to surface design considerations before implementing in unfamiliar domains.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: When should you fix multiple issues in one message versus sequentially?
cards.back: Single message when fixes interact; sequential iteration when issues are independent.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5

cards.front: A migration script mishandles null edge cases. How should you iterate with Claude?
cards.back: Provide specific test cases with example input and expected output for the failing edge case.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 3.5: Provide specific test cases with example input and expected output for the failing edge case.

cards.front: A CI job hangs because Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. How do you fix that?
cards.back: Use -p (or --print) flag for non-interactive mode: process prompt, output result, exit.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6; Sample Q10
cards.rationale: -p (--print) is the documented non-interactive CI mode: process, output, exit. CLAUDE_HEADLESS, --batch, and stdin tricks are not the correct Claude Code approach.

cards.front: Which CLI flags post structured PR review findings as inline comments from CI?
cards.back: --output-format json with --json-schema for machine-parseable structured findings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6
cards.rationale: --output-format json with --json-schema produces machine-parseable findings so CI can post inline PR comments. This is not a review-architecture question.

cards.front: How do you provide project context to Claude Code invoked from CI?
cards.back: CLAUDE.md with testing standards, fixture conventions, and review criteria loaded automatically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: Why use an independent Claude instance to review code it generated in the same session?
cards.back: Session context isolation—generator retains reasoning context and is less likely to question its own decisions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6

cards.front: When re-running a PR review after new commits, how do you avoid duplicate inline comments?
cards.back: Include prior review findings in context; instruct Claude to report only new or still-unaddressed issues.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6
cards.rationale: Pass prior findings back in and instruct Claude to report only new or still-open issues so re-runs do not spam duplicate comments.

cards.front: CI test generation suggests scenarios already in the suite. What context should you add?
cards.back: Provide existing test files in context so generation avoids duplicate coverage.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6
cards.rationale: Put existing test files in context so generation does not propose coverage the suite already has.

cards.front: How do you reduce low-value generated tests in Claude Code?
cards.back: Document testing standards, valuable test criteria, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6
cards.rationale: Document testing standards, what a valuable test looks like, and available fixtures in CLAUDE.md so CI generation produces fewer low-value tests.

cards.front: When running Claude Code in CI for PR review, what configuration concerns matter most?
cards.back: Non-interactive (-p), explicit permissions, structured/deterministic outputs, independent review instance—not open-ended agent runs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6
cards.rationale: CI needs -p (non-interactive), tight permissions, structured output, and an independent review instance—not an open-ended interactive agent.

cards.front: Name two CI non-interactive flags that do not exist for Claude Code.
cards.back: CLAUDE_HEADLESS env var and --batch flag—use -p/--print instead.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.6; Sample Q10

cards.front: What are the primary domains for the Code Generation scenario (Scenario 2)?
cards.back: D3 (Claude Code config/workflows) and D5 (context management/reliability).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What are the primary domains for the CI/CD with Claude Code scenario (Scenario 5)?
cards.back: D3 (Claude Code) and D4 (prompt engineering/structured output for review findings).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Scenario 2 involves slash commands, CLAUDE.md, and plan mode. What skill is the exam testing?
cards.back: Integrating Claude Code into dev workflow: team config, custom commands, and when to plan vs execute directly.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 2

cards.front: What is an example path-scoped rule that applies only to Terraform files?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ file with frontmatter paths: ["terraform/**/*"] loading only when editing matching files.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3

cards.front: Put all area conventions in root CLAUDE.md headers—rely on Claude to infer which applies. Why unreliable?
cards.back: Relies on inference vs explicit path matching—rules with glob patterns give deterministic automatic application.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6

cards.front: For a monolith-to-microservices split, why is direct execution with comprehensive upfront structure instructions wrong?
cards.back: Assumes structure without codebase exploration—dependencies discovered late cause costly rework; plan first.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.4; Sample Q5

cards.front: Why is auto-applying conventions via skills in .claude/skills/ insufficient compared with path rules?
cards.back: Skills require manual invocation or model choice—not deterministic path-based automatic application.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.3; Sample Q6

cards.front: In test-driven iteration before implementation, what should the tests cover?
cards.back: Expected behavior, edge cases, and performance requirements—iterate by sharing failures with Claude.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.5
cards.rationale: iterate by sharing failures with Claude.

cards.front: Besides verbose codebase analysis, what is another use case for context: fork on skills?
cards.back: Exploratory brainstorming of alternatives—isolates speculative output from the main session.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D3, Task 3.2
cards.rationale: isolates speculative output from the main session.

cards.front: What are the primary domains for the Developer Productivity scenario (Scenario 4)?
cards.back: D2 (built-in tools + MCP), D3 (Claude Code workflows), D1 (delegation/orchestration).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: Why should you use structured output (JSON schema) instead of parsing free-text responses?
cards.back: Enables validation, automated retries on failure, and downstream automation without fragile regex on prose.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/build-with-claude/structured-outputs

cards.front: Why are explicit review criteria better than vague instructions like 'be conservative'?
cards.back: Specific categorical criteria (flag when comment contradicts code) beat vague confidence filtering for precision.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: Automated review has high false positives in one category, and developers ignore all findings. What should you do first?
cards.back: Temporarily disable the high false-positive category to restore trust while improving prompts for that category.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1
cards.rationale: High false positives in one category destroy trust in every category. Disable that category while you tighten its prompt, then turn it back on.

cards.front: How do you define consistent severity levels in automated code review prompts?
cards.back: Explicit severity criteria with concrete code examples for each level—not generic confidence thresholds.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1
cards.rationale: not generic confidence thresholds.

cards.front: Why do high false-positive rates in one review category hurt the whole system?
cards.back: Developers lose trust and dismiss accurate findings in other categories too.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: How should a review prompt distinguish bugs and security issues from minor style nits?
cards.back: Define explicit categories to report versus skip—don't rely on confidence-based filtering alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1
cards.rationale: don't rely on confidence-based filtering alone.

cards.front: When are few-shot examples most effective?
cards.back: When detailed instructions alone produce inconsistent format or ambiguous-case handling—enables generalization to novel patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Review output format is inconsistent (location, severity, fix). How should you improve it?
cards.back: Few-shot examples demonstrating exact desired format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: Few-shot examples of the exact format (location, issue, severity, suggested fix) beat more prose instructions when structure is inconsistent.

cards.front: How do you reduce false positives in review while still catching real bugs?
cards.back: Few-shot examples distinguishing acceptable local patterns from genuine issues—shows reasoning for each.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: shows reasoning for each.

cards.front: Extraction fails on varied document layouts (inline citations versus bibliographies). How do you fix that?
cards.back: Few-shot examples showing correct handling of each document structure variant.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 4.2: Few-shot examples showing correct handling of each document structure variant.

cards.front: The model returns null or empty required fields on varied formats. What few-shot approach should you use?
cards.back: Examples demonstrating correct extraction from each format variant—not just schema tightening alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: not just schema tightening alone.

cards.front: How many few-shot examples should you use for ambiguous scenarios, and what should they show?
cards.back: 2–4 targeted examples with reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 4.2: 2–4 targeted examples with reasoning for why one action was chosen over plausible alternatives.

cards.front: What is the most reliable approach for guaranteed schema-compliant JSON output?
cards.back: tool_use with JSON schemas—eliminates JSON syntax errors vs free-text JSON generation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3

cards.front: Strict JSON schemas via tool_use eliminate syntax errors—but what errors remain?
cards.back: Semantic errors: wrong field values, line items not summing to total, values in incorrect fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3–4.4

cards.front: The source document may omit a field. How should you design the schema to prevent fabrication?
cards.back: Make fields optional/nullable when information may be absent—don't require fields the source lacks.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: don't require fields the source lacks.

cards.front: What schema pattern should you use for an extensible category field?
cards.back: Enum with "other" plus a detail string field for categories not in the predefined list.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: Use an enum plus an 'other' value and a detail string so unknown categories are captured instead of forced into a wrong bucket.

cards.front: Source data can be ambiguous. How should you design the extraction enum?
cards.back: Add enum value like "unclear" for ambiguous cases rather than forcing a wrong category.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 4.3: Add enum value like "unclear" for ambiguous cases rather than forcing a wrong category.

cards.front: Source documents have inconsistent date formats, but the output schema is strict. What should you do?
cards.back: Include format normalization rules in the prompt alongside the strict output schema.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: Keep the output schema strict, and put date-normalization rules in the prompt so inconsistent source formats still map to one output shape.

cards.front: You have multiple extraction schemas and the document type is unknown at request time. How should you set tool_choice?
cards.back: tool_choice: "any" to guarantee structured tool output instead of conversational text.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: tool_choice "any" guarantees a tool call when several extraction schemas exist and the document type is unknown—auto may return chat text instead.

cards.front: Where do you extract structured data from a tool_use extraction call?
cards.back: From the tool_use response block—schema defines tool input parameters; model fills structured fields there.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3
cards.rationale: schema defines tool input parameters; model fills structured fields there.

cards.front: What is retry-with-error-feedback for extraction?
cards.back: On validation failure, send follow-up with original document, failed extraction, and specific validation errors for self-correction.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: When do validation retries succeed, and when do they fail?
cards.back: Succeed on format/structural mismatches. Fail when required info is absent from source (or only in external doc not provided).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: How do schema syntax errors differ from semantic validation errors?
cards.back: Syntax errors eliminated by tool_use strict schemas; semantic errors need cross-field rules (totals, field placement).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4

cards.front: Developers dismiss many automated findings. How should you design the feedback loop?
cards.back: Add detected_pattern field to findings to analyze which constructs trigger false positives when dismissed.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 4.4: Add detected_pattern field to findings to analyze which constructs trigger false positives when dismissed.

cards.front: How should extraction self-correct when invoice totals do not add up?
cards.back: Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and flag discrepancies; add conflict_detected for inconsistent source data.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 4.4: Extract calculated_total alongside stated_total and flag discrepancies; add conflict_detected for inconsistent source data.

cards.front: Extraction misses nullable fields intermittently. What is the best improvement?
cards.back: Tighten required vs optional schema, validation-retry loop, and explicit examples for null/edge cases.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3–4.4; Structured Extraction scenario
cards.rationale: Mark truly optional fields nullable, retry with validation errors, and add few-shot null/edge examples. Tightening every field to required causes fabrication.

cards.front: What are the cost and latency tradeoffs of the Message Batches API?
cards.back: 50% cost savings, up to 24-hour processing window, no guaranteed latency SLA.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Appendix

cards.front: Should you use the Batch API for both a pre-merge blocking check and an overnight technical-debt report?
cards.back: Batch only for latency-tolerant jobs (overnight reports); keep synchronous API for blocking pre-merge checks.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Sample Q11
cards.rationale: Message Batches save cost but lack latency SLA—fine for overnight reports, unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks. Polling batches for merge gates is unacceptable; custom_id correlates batch results; timeout fallback adds complexity vs matching API to workflow latency needs.

cards.front: What is the Message Batches API limitation on tool calling?
cards.back: No multi-turn tool calling within a single batch request—cannot execute tools mid-request and return results.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: What is the purpose of custom_id in the Message Batches API?
cards.back: Correlate batch request/response pairs and identify failed documents for resubmission.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5

cards.front: How should you resubmit failed documents from a batch job?
cards.back: Resubmit only failed documents by custom_id with modifications (e.g., chunk oversized docs that exceeded context).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5
cards.rationale: Resubmit only failed custom_id items, with fixes such as chunking docs that exceeded context. Do not resubmit the whole batch.

cards.front: Before batch-processing 10,000 documents, what cost-reduction step should you take first?
cards.back: Refine prompts on a sample set first to maximize first-pass success and reduce resubmission costs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5
cards.rationale: Refine prompts on a sample before 10k documents so first-pass success is high and you avoid expensive resubmission loops.

cards.front: Why is self-review of generated code in the same session limited?
cards.back: Model retains generation reasoning context—less likely to question its own decisions than an independent reviewer.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: What is the best approach to catch subtle issues in AI-generated code?
cards.back: Second independent Claude instance reviewing without the generator's reasoning context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6
cards.rationale: A second Claude instance without the generator's reasoning context catches subtle bugs better than same-session self-review or extended thinking alone.

cards.front: For a large multi-file PR review, what multi-pass architecture should you use?
cards.back: Per-file passes for local issues plus separate integration pass for cross-file data flow.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6; Sample Q12
cards.rationale: Split reviews into per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass—fixes attention dilution across many files. Splitting PRs burdens developers; larger context does not fix attention quality; consensus across passes would suppress intermittently caught bugs.

cards.front: How should you route automated review findings to human triage?
cards.back: Run a verification pass where the model reports confidence alongside each finding, then route using calibrated thresholds (high-severity / low-confidence to humans).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6
cards.rationale: Task 4.6 uses a verification pass with self-reported confidence for calibrated routing. That is different from using uncalibrated confidence as an escalation trigger in support.

cards.front: When should PR findings be prompt-only versus JSON schema for CI gates?
cards.back: Schema for machine consumption (CI gates, dashboards); prompts alone only for human-readable narrative.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.3; CI/CD scenario

cards.front: Why is it a problem to trust model self-reported confidence without validation?
cards.back: Not calibrated by default—use schema checks, cross-field rules, or human review thresholds for high-risk fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.4; D5 crossover

cards.front: Why is it wrong to run three full PR review passes and only flag issues that appear in two or more?
cards.back: Suppresses real bugs caught intermittently—consensus filtering hides attention-dilution problems; split passes instead.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6; Sample Q12

cards.front: What are the primary domains for the Structured Data Extraction scenario (Scenario 6)?
cards.back: D4 (schemas, validation, batch) and D5 (reliability, human review for low confidence).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What extraction-system requirements does the exam guide list for Scenario 6?
cards.back: Extract from unstructured docs, validate with JSON schemas, handle edge cases, integrate with downstream systems.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 6

cards.front: What extraction use cases benefit from few-shot examples to reduce hallucination?
cards.back: Informal measurements, varied document structures, and inconsistent field formats in source documents.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: Why is switching blocking pre-merge checks to the Batch API with status polling wrong?
cards.back: Batch has no latency SLA—unacceptable for workflows where developers wait to merge.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Sample Q11

cards.front: You have a 30-hour SLA and batches can take up to 24 hours. How often should you submit batches?
cards.back: Calculate submission windows (e.g., 4-hour intervals) so batches complete within SLA with margin for retries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5
cards.rationale: Batches can take up to 24 hours. For a 30-hour SLA, submit on a shorter cadence (for example every 4 hours) so there is margin for retries.

cards.front: Why prefer independent review instances over extended thinking for self-review?
cards.back: Independent instances without generator context catch more subtle issues than self-review instructions or extended thinking alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6

cards.front: What is an example of explicit review criteria for comments versus code?
cards.back: Flag comments only when claimed behavior contradicts actual code—not vague 'check comment accuracy'.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.1

cards.front: How do few-shot examples generalize beyond the cases you pre-specify?
cards.back: Demonstrate judgment and reasoning on ambiguous examples so the model applies similar logic to novel patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2

cards.front: How should few-shot examples teach the model to report branch-level test coverage gaps?
cards.back: Show how to identify and report coverage gaps at branch level—ambiguous case requiring demonstrated judgment.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.2
cards.rationale: ambiguous case requiring demonstrated judgment.

cards.front: Why is switching both blocking and overnight jobs to the Batch API with a real-time fallback over-engineered?
cards.back: Match API to latency needs—sync for blocking checks, batch for overnight; fallback adds unnecessary complexity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.5; Sample Q11

cards.front: For a large PR review, why is switching to a higher-tier model with a larger context window insufficient?
cards.back: Larger context doesn't fix attention dilution—split into per-file plus integration passes instead.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D4, Task 4.6; Sample Q12

cards.front: What is context degradation in long agent sessions?
cards.back: Reasoning quality drops as irrelevant history accumulates—inconsistent answers and vague 'typical pattern' references instead of specifics.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: What is the risk of progressive summarization in long support sessions?
cards.back: Condenses amounts, dates, percentages, and customer-stated expectations into vague summaries—loses critical transactional facts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: What is the 'lost in the middle' effect?
cards.back: Models reliably use info at the start and end of long inputs but may omit findings buried in middle sections.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: How do you preserve order amounts and dates across a long support conversation?
cards.back: Extract transactional facts into a persistent case facts block in each prompt—outside summarized history.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: Keep amounts, dates, and order IDs in a persistent case-facts block outside summarized history so progressive summarization cannot wash them out.

cards.front: Order lookup returns 40+ fields but only 5 matter for returns. How should you fix the context?
cards.back: Trim verbose tool outputs to relevant fields before they accumulate in conversation context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: Trim 40-field order payloads to the few return-relevant fields before they accumulate. Verbose tool results crowd out the facts that matter.

cards.front: How do you mitigate lost-in-the-middle when aggregating subagent results?
cards.back: Place key findings summary at the beginning; organize detailed results with explicit section headers.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 5.1: Place key findings summary at the beginning; organize detailed results with explicit section headers.

cards.front: The downstream synthesis agent has a limited context budget. How should upstream agents shape their output?
cards.back: Return structured key facts, citations, and relevance scores—not verbose reasoning chains.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: When downstream context is tight, upstream agents should return key facts, citations, and relevance scores—not long reasoning chains.

cards.front: Why should you pass complete conversation history in subsequent API requests?
cards.back: Maintains conversational coherence—the model needs prior turns to reason about the ongoing case.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1

cards.front: A support session covers multiple issues (billing and a return). How should you structure the context layer?
cards.back: Persist structured issue data (order IDs, amounts, statuses) in a separate context layer for each concern.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: For billing plus a return, persist structured issue data (IDs, amounts, statuses) in a separate layer per concern so one summary does not merge them.

cards.front: Name three appropriate escalation triggers besides calling the case 'complex'.
cards.back: Customer explicitly requests human, policy exception/gap, and inability to make meaningful progress.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: First-contact resolution is 55%: the agent escalates easy cases and handles hard policy exceptions alone. What is the best calibration fix?
cards.back: Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples showing escalate vs resolve autonomously.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3
cards.rationale: Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples fix unclear decision boundaries—the proportionate first fix. LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated on hard cases; a separate classifier is over-engineered before prompt tuning; sentiment does not measure case complexity.

cards.front: Why is routing to a human when self-reported confidence is below a threshold unreliable?
cards.back: LLM confidence is poorly calibrated—agent may be wrongly confident on hard cases and uncertain on easy ones.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: Why is escalating on a negative-sentiment threshold the wrong calibration fix?
cards.back: Sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity—the actual issue is unclear escalation boundaries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: The customer explicitly demands a human agent. What should the agent do?
cards.back: Honor immediately—do not attempt investigation first when they explicitly request a human.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2
cards.rationale: do not attempt investigation first when they explicitly request a human.

cards.front: The customer is frustrated, but the issue is within the agent's capability. What should the agent do?
cards.back: Acknowledge frustration and offer resolution; escalate only if customer reiterates preference for human.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2
cards.rationale: Frustration alone is not an escalation trigger if the issue is in scope. Acknowledge, offer to resolve, and escalate only if they still want a human.

cards.front: Policy is silent on competitor price matching (it only covers own-site adjustments). What should the agent do?
cards.back: Escalate—policy gap/exception case, not autonomous resolution.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2
cards.rationale: policy gap/exception case, not autonomous resolution.

cards.front: get_customer returns multiple matches. What should the agent do?
cards.back: Ask for additional identifiers—never pick a match heuristically.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2
cards.rationale: never pick a match heuristically.

cards.front: Subagents need prior search results. What is the best way to pass that context?
cards.back: Explicit structured handoffs (IDs, snippets, citations) via coordinator—not implicit shared memory.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1; Multi-Agent Research scenario
cards.rationale: not implicit shared memory.

cards.front: The web search subagent times out. What error context should you propagate to the coordinator?
cards.back: Structured context: failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternative approaches.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3; Sample Q8
cards.rationale: Structured error context enables coordinator recovery (retry, alternate query, partial results). Generic retry status hides context; marking failure as success blocks recovery; terminating the whole workflow is unnecessary when partial progress exists.

cards.front: Why is it an anti-pattern for a subagent to return empty results marked successful after a timeout?
cards.back: Silently suppresses errors—coordinator cannot recover or annotate coverage gaps.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3; Sample Q8

cards.front: After partial subagent failures, what should synthesis output include?
cards.back: Coverage annotations: which findings are well-supported vs which topic areas have gaps from unavailable sources.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 5.3: Coverage annotations: which findings are well-supported vs which topic areas have gaps from unavailable sources.

cards.front: The agent loop fails twice on the same tool error. What should you do next?
cards.back: Escalate or change strategy (alternate tool, human handoff)—not infinite identical retries.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3
cards.rationale: not infinite identical retries.

cards.front: What is the purpose of scratchpad files in long Claude Code exploration sessions?
cards.back: Persist key findings across context boundaries; reference for later questions to counteract degradation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Verbose codebase exploration fills the context. Which Claude Code command reduces usage?
cards.back: /compact to condense verbose discovery output during extended sessions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4; Appendix
cards.rationale: /compact condenses verbose discovery output in long Claude Code sessions. It is the documented command for context pressure during exploration.

cards.front: In multi-phase codebase exploration, how should you manage context between phases?
cards.back: Summarize key findings from one phase, inject summary into context before spawning subagents for the next.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4
cards.rationale: Summarize each exploration phase and inject that summary before the next subagents spawn so later phases do not inherit a huge raw trace.

cards.front: What crash-recovery pattern should multi-agent workflows use?
cards.back: Each agent exports state to a known location; coordinator loads manifest on resume and injects into prompts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4

cards.front: Why is dumping the entire repo into context for every Claude Code task a problem?
cards.back: Wastes tokens and adds noise—use Grep/Glob and scoped reads incrementally.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4; D2 Task 2.5

cards.front: Overall extraction accuracy is 97%. Why should you not automate away all human review?
cards.back: Aggregate metrics may mask poor performance on specific document types or individual fields.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5

cards.front: How should you monitor quality for high-confidence extractions over time?
