cards.back: Stratified random sampling to measure error rates and detect novel error patterns.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 5.5: Stratified random sampling to measure error rates and detect novel error patterns.

cards.front: How do you calibrate human-review routing for extractions?
cards.back: Model outputs field-level confidence; calibrate thresholds using labeled validation sets.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5
cards.rationale: Have the model emit field-level confidence, then set review thresholds on a labeled validation set. Uncalibrated scores are not production routing rules.

cards.front: Before reducing human review on high-confidence extractions, what should you verify?
cards.back: Accuracy by document type and field segment—consistent performance across all segments.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5
cards.rationale: consistent performance across all segments.

cards.front: Reviewer capacity is limited. Which extractions should you prioritize for human review?
cards.back: Low model confidence, ambiguous source documents, or contradictory source data.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.5
cards.rationale: With limited reviewers, send low-confidence extractions and ambiguous or contradictory source documents to humans first.

cards.front: How is source attribution lost in multi-agent research pipelines?
cards.back: Summarization compresses findings without preserving claim-to-source mappings.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6

cards.front: What provenance must subagent output include for downstream synthesis?
cards.back: Structured claim-source mappings (URLs, document names, excerpts) preserved through synthesis.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 5.6: Structured claim-source mappings (URLs, document names, excerpts) preserved through synthesis.

cards.front: Two credible sources report different statistics. How should synthesis handle that?
cards.back: Annotate conflict with source attribution—do not arbitrarily pick one value.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: do not arbitrarily pick one value.

cards.front: Why should structured subagent outputs include publication or collection dates?
cards.back: Enables correct temporal interpretation—prevents time differences being misread as contradictions.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: prevents time differences being misread as contradictions.

cards.front: How should a research report structure contested findings versus established ones?
cards.back: Explicit sections distinguishing well-established findings from contested ones with methodological context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: Structure the report with explicit well-established vs contested sections and keep methodological context. Do not flatten everything into one confident narrative.

cards.front: How should synthesis format mixed content types?
cards.back: Render appropriately—financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists.

cards.front: Which exam scenarios list D5 as a primary domain?
cards.back: Four: Customer Support, Code Generation, Multi-Agent Research, and Structured Data Extraction. Developer Productivity and CI/CD do not list D5 as primary.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — scenario map

cards.front: What D5 focus areas does the Code Generation scenario (Scenario 2) emphasize?
cards.back: Context preservation across edits, plan vs execute context management, and session reliability.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 2

cards.front: What metadata must structured subagent outputs include for downstream synthesis?
cards.back: Dates, source locations, and methodological context—not just claims without provenance context.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.1
cards.rationale: not just claims without provenance context.

cards.front: Why is deploying a classifier to predict escalation before the agent runs an over-engineered first step?
cards.back: Requires labeled data and ML infra when prompt criteria with few-shot hasn't been tried yet.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2; Sample Q3

cards.front: A subagent retries, then returns generic 'search unavailable' to the coordinator. What is the problem?
cards.back: Hides failure type, attempted query, and partial results—coordinator cannot make informed recovery.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3; Sample Q8

cards.front: A single subagent failure terminates the entire multi-agent workflow. Why is that wrong?
cards.back: Often recoverable with partial results, alternate queries, or gap annotations—unnecessary full termination.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.3

cards.front: During long codebase exploration, how do you delegate specific questions while preserving coordination?
cards.back: Spawn subagents for focused tasks (find test files, trace refund flow) while main agent keeps high-level coordination.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4
cards.rationale: Exam judgment aligned to task 5.4: Spawn subagents for focused tasks (find test files, trace refund flow) while main agent keeps high-level coordination.

cards.front: Document analysis finds conflicting values from sources. What should happen before synthesis?
cards.back: Complete analysis with conflicts included and explicitly annotated—let coordinator reconcile before passing to synthesis.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.6
cards.rationale: let coordinator reconcile before passing to synthesis.

cards.front: How should you use a scratchpad file during exploration for follow-up questions?
cards.back: Record key findings in scratchpad; reference it for subsequent questions to counteract context degradation.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.4
cards.rationale: Write key findings to a scratchpad and reread it on follow-up questions so later turns do not fall back on vague 'typical patterns'.

cards.front: What is the official exam code for Claude Certified Architect, Foundations?
cards.back: CCAR-F (also written CCA-F or CCAF in older materials).
cards.rationale: Pearson lists CCAR-F as the current code.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide
https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/about-claude/models

cards.front: How many questions, how much time, and what passing score does CCAR-F use?
cards.back: 60 items in 120 minutes; pass at scaled 720 on a 100–1000 scale. Items are multiple-choice or multiple-response (each item says how many to select).
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide

cards.front: How many scenarios appear on the exam, and from what pool?
cards.back: 4 scenarios per exam, drawn randomly from a published bank of 6.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide

cards.front: When a scenario needs deterministic guarantees (money, identity, or schema compliance), what should you prefer?
cards.back: Prefer structural/programmatic fixes (hooks, prerequisites, scoped tools, tool_use schemas) over prompt-only instructions.
cards.rationale: Exam tests judgment: prompts are insufficient for hard guarantees.
sources: Community study guides aligned to Exam Guide patterns
Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — sample rationales

cards.front: Sample Q1 (Customer Support): Why does a programmatic prerequisite beat a prompt, few-shot examples, or routing when get_customer is skipped?
cards.back: Blocks lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns verified ID—deterministic enforcement for identity before refunds.
cards.rationale: Programmatic enforcement gives deterministic guarantees for required tool sequences; prompt and few-shot rely on probabilistic LLM compliance—insufficient when misidentification causes financial harm. Routing classifiers change tool availability, not ordering.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q1

cards.front: Sample Q2 (Customer Support): Why should you expand tool descriptions before adding few-shot examples, routing, or consolidating tools?
cards.back: Descriptions are the primary LLM tool-selection signal—add inputs, examples, edge cases, and boundaries vs similar tools.
cards.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary selection mechanism; minimal descriptions cause confusion between similar tools. Few-shot adds tokens without fixing descriptions; routing is over-engineered for a first step; consolidation is valid but higher effort.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q2

cards.front: Sample Q3 (Customer Support): Why do explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples beat confidence scores, classifiers, or sentiment?
cards.back: Fix unclear escalate-vs-resolve boundaries—the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure.
cards.rationale: Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples fix unclear decision boundaries. LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated on hard cases; a separate classifier is over-engineered before prompt tuning; sentiment does not measure case complexity.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q3

cards.front: Sample Q4 (Code Generation): Where should a team-shared /review slash command live?
cards.back: .claude/commands/ in the project repository—version-controlled for everyone who clones the repo.
cards.rationale: Project slash commands live in .claude/commands/ and are version-controlled. ~/.claude/commands/ is personal; CLAUDE.md holds instructions not command definitions; .claude/config.json is not the Claude Code command mechanism.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q4

cards.front: Sample Q5 (Code Generation): For a monolith-to-microservices split across dozens of files, why start in plan mode?
cards.back: Explore dependencies and design service boundaries before editing—large architectural scope is already stated.
cards.rationale: Plan mode fits large architectural work with exploration before edits. Direct execution risks rework when dependencies are unknown; rigid upfront instructions skip discovery; waiting for emergent complexity ignores stated large-scale scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q5

cards.front: Sample Q6 (Code Generation): Tests are spread as *.test.tsx. Why use .claude/rules/ with globs?
cards.back: Glob patterns (e.g. **/*.test.tsx) auto-apply conventions by path regardless of directory.
cards.rationale: .claude/rules/ with glob patterns apply conventions by file path—including tests spread across directories. Root CLAUDE.md relies on inference; skills need invocation; per-directory CLAUDE.md cannot cover scattered test files.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q6

cards.front: Sample Q7 (Multi-Agent Research): The report covers only visual arts. Why is coordinator decomposition the root cause?
cards.back: Logs show narrow subtasks (digital art, graphic design, photography)—subagents succeeded within assigned scope.
cards.rationale: Coordinator logs show decomposition into only visual-arts subtasks—subagents succeeded within narrow assignments. Downstream agents are not the root cause; synthesis, search, and analysis worked within assigned scope.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q7

cards.front: Sample Q8 (Multi-Agent Research): The search subagent times out. Why return structured error context to the coordinator?
cards.back: Return failure type, attempted query, partial results, and alternatives so coordinator can recover intelligently.
cards.rationale: Structured error context enables coordinator recovery (retry, alternate query, partial results). Generic retry status hides context; marking failure as success blocks recovery; terminating the whole workflow is unnecessary when partial progress exists.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q8

cards.front: Sample Q9 (Multi-Agent Research): 85% of checks are simple facts. Why give synthesis a scoped verify_fact tool?
cards.back: Least privilege for common lookups; complex verification still routes through coordinator to search agent.
cards.rationale: Scoped verify_fact on synthesis covers simple fact-checks while complex work stays with search via coordinator—least privilege. End-of-pass batching creates blocking dependencies; giving synthesis all search tools over-provisions; speculative caching cannot predict verification needs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q9

cards.front: Sample Q10 (CI/CD): The pipeline hangs waiting for input. Why use the -p flag?
cards.back: claude -p runs non-interactive: process prompt, output to stdout, exit—required for CI/CD.
cards.rationale: -p (--print) is the documented non-interactive CI mode. CLAUDE_HEADLESS, --batch, and stdin tricks are not the correct Claude Code approach.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q10

cards.front: Sample Q11: Why use the Batch API only for overnight jobs, not for pre-merge checks?
cards.back: Batches save ~50% cost but lack latency SLA—unsuitable for blocking merge gates.
cards.rationale: Message Batches save cost but lack latency SLA—fine for overnight reports, unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks. Polling batches for merge gates is unacceptable; custom_id correlates batch results; timeout fallback adds complexity vs matching API to workflow latency needs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q11

cards.front: Sample Q12 (CI/CD): A 14-file PR review is inconsistent. Why split into per-file and integration passes?
cards.back: Per-file local analysis then cross-file integration pass—fixes attention dilution across many files.
cards.rationale: Split reviews into per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass—fixes attention dilution. Splitting PRs burdens developers; larger context does not fix attention quality; consensus across passes would suppress intermittently caught bugs.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Section 9, Sample Q12

cards.front: [Customer Support · 1/5] You deploy a support agent with MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human). Target is 80%+ first-contact resolution. What architectural foundation comes first?
cards.back: Design agentic loop with stop_reason control, scoped tools, and escalation paths—before tuning prompts.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1
Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.1

cards.front: [Customer Support · 2/5] Production data: 12% of cases skip get_customer and call lookup_order by name only, causing wrong refunds. What is the best fix?
cards.back: Programmatic prerequisite blocking lookup_order and process_refund until get_customer returns verified customer ID.
cards.rationale: Money and identity need deterministic enforcement—not prompts alone.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1; Sample Q1
Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D1, Task 1.4

cards.front: [Customer Support · 3/5] Logs show get_customer called for order queries (#12345) instead of lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions. What should you fix first?
cards.back: Expand tool descriptions with inputs, example queries, edge cases, and when to use each vs similar tools.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1; Sample Q2
Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D2, Task 2.1

cards.front: [Customer Support · 4/5] First-contact resolution is 55%: the agent escalates easy cases and handles hard policy exceptions alone. What is the best calibration fix?
cards.back: Add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples for escalate vs resolve autonomously.
sources: Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — Scenario 1; Sample Q3
Official CCAR-F Exam Guide — D5, Task 5.2

cards.front: [Customer Support · 5/5] get_customer returns multiple matches for one name. What must the agent do?
cards.back: Ask for additional identifiers—never select a match heuristically.

cards.front: [Code Generation · 1/5] Your team uses Claude Code for generation, refactoring, and docs—with slash commands, CLAUDE.md, and plan mode. What should be shared via git for consistent team behavior?

cards.front: [Code Generation · 2/5] You need a /review slash command available to everyone who clones the repo. Where do you put it?

cards.front: [Code Generation · 3/5] Assignment: split a monolith into microservices across dozens of files with unclear boundaries. Which mode should you use first?

cards.front: [Code Generation · 4/5] Tests live as *.test.tsx next to components across the repo. How do you auto-apply test conventions when generating code?
cards.back: .claude/rules/ with glob paths like **/*.test.tsx—not directory-bound CLAUDE.md or inference from headers.

cards.front: [Code Generation · 5/5] In a long refactor session, the model starts citing generic patterns instead of files it read earlier. How do you mitigate that?

cards.front: [Multi-Agent Research · 1/5] Coordinator delegates search, document analysis, synthesis, and report agents. What must allowedTools include on the coordinator?

cards.front: [Multi-Agent Research · 2/5] Topic is 'AI in creative industries', but the final report covers only visual arts because the coordinator assigned digital art, graphic design, and photography only. What is the root cause?

cards.front: [Multi-Agent Research · 3/5] Web search subagent times out. What should the coordinator receive?

cards.front: [Multi-Agent Research · 4/5] Synthesis needs many simple fact-checks (85%) but some deep searches (15%). How do you reduce latency without over-provisioning synthesis?

cards.front: [Multi-Agent Research · 5/5] The final report must preserve citations through synthesis. What should you require from subagents?

cards.front: [Developer Productivity · 1/5] An agent helps engineers explore legacy codebases using built-in tools and MCP. When should you prefer MCP over Grep or Glob?

cards.front: [Developer Productivity · 2/5] You need all callers of a function across the monorepo. Which built-in tool should you use first?

cards.front: [Developer Productivity · 3/5] The agent prefers Grep over your team's richer MCP code-search tool. How do you fix that?

cards.front: [Developer Productivity · 4/5] How should you explore a large codebase without reading every file?

cards.front: [CI/CD · 2/5] How do you post structured findings as inline PR comments from CI?

cards.front: [CI/CD · 3/5] The same Claude session generated the code and then reviews it, missing subtle bugs. What is a better approach?

cards.front: [CI/CD · 4/5] A 14-file PR review has inconsistent depth, missed bugs, and contradictory feedback. How should you restructure it?

cards.front: [CI/CD · 5/5] Re-running the review after new commits duplicates inline comments. What context should you add?

cards.front: [Structured Extraction · 1/5] A pipeline extracts from unstructured docs, validates with JSON schema, and integrates downstream. What is the most reliable structured-output approach?

cards.front: [Structured Extraction · 2/5] Source docs often omit optional fields, and the model fabricates values. How should you fix the schema?

cards.front: [Structured Extraction · 3/5] Validation fails on a date format mismatch, but the information exists in the document. What is the next step?

cards.front: [Structured Extraction · 4/5] A manager wants the Batch API for pre-merge blocking checks and overnight reports. How should you split those jobs?
